name: Number System, Surds & Roots
analogy: A surd like √2 is a number that refuses to be written neatly as a fraction — like a length that never lands exactly on a ruler mark. **Rationalising** just tidies the fraction so the messy root sits on top, not underneath.
explain: Numbers split into natural, integer, rational and irrational. A perfect square has every prime factor to an even power; a perfect cube has every prime factor to a power that is a multiple of three. To simplify a surd fraction, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
formulas: Perfect square ⇒ every prime power is even
Perfect cube ⇒ every prime power is a multiple of 3

variant.q: Smallest number that 1176 must be multiplied by to become a perfect square?
variant.solution: 1176 = 2³·3·7². The 2³ needs one more 2 and the lone 3 needs another 3 ⇒ ×6 = 7056 = 84².

name: HCF & LCM
analogy: **HCF** is the largest identical tile that paves two rooms exactly. **LCM** is the soonest two blinking lights flash together again.
explain: HCF is the biggest number dividing both; LCM is the smallest number both divide into. The product of any two numbers equals HCF × LCM, which instantly gives a missing number.
formulas: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
Divisibility add/subtract: find the nearest multiple

variant.q: HCF of two numbers is 8 and LCM is 96. One number is 24. The other?

name: Simplification (BODMAS)
analogy: Like following a recipe's steps in order — you cream the butter before you bake, never after. And 'of' is sneaky: it means multiply.
explain: Resolve in order: Brackets, Of, Division & Multiplication (left to right), then Addition & Subtraction. Spot a³+b³ / a³−b³ patterns to dodge ugly cube arithmetic.
formulas: B · O · D · M · A · S

variant.q: Simplify: 12 + 8 × 3 − 6 ÷ 2

name: Ratio & Proportion
analogy: A recipe scaled up keeps the same ratio of flour to sugar. To chain a:b and b:c, make the shared term b equal in both — like matching gears so they mesh.
explain: Convert a ratio to 'parts', find the value of one part, then scale. To combine a:b and b:c, scale each so b is the same number.
formulas: Total = sum of all ratio parts
Chain a:b & b:c by equalising b

variant.q: If a:b = 3:4 and b:c = 6:7, then a:c?

name: Percentage
analogy: A 20% rise then a 20% fall does NOT cancel — you end lower, because the fall is taken on a bigger number. Percentage changes multiply, they never add.
explain: Percent means 'per hundred'. For successive changes, multiply the growth factors. Pass/fail and election problems are just percentages of a hidden total.
formulas: Find total when a % is known, then scale

variant.q: A number rises 25% then falls 20%. Net change?

name: Profit & Loss
analogy: The 'sticker price' is the marked price; what you actually pay after the sale is the selling price. Profit and loss are always measured against the cost price, never the marked price.
explain: Profit% and loss% use cost price as the base. Discount comes off the marked price. When two items sell at the same price with equal % gain and loss, there is always a net loss.

variant.q: An article sold at 20% profit fetches ₹600. Its cost price?

name: Simple Interest
analogy: Rent that is the same every month, no matter how long you stay — the interest is always on the original amount only.
explain: Simple interest grows by a fixed amount each year on the principal alone. If the money doubles, the interest equals the principal, so rate × time = 100.
formulas: SI = a fraction of P ⇒ solve for T

variant.q: Find the simple interest on ₹4000 at 6% for 3 years.

name: Compound Interest
analogy: A snowball rolling downhill — it grows faster and faster because each new layer sits on a bigger ball. Interest earns interest.
explain: Compound interest applies the rate to the new balance each period. For half-yearly, halve the rate and double the periods. The amount after each year forms a constant ratio.

variant.q: Compound interest on ₹10000 at 10% for 2 years?

name: Averages
analogy: Pouring water of different heights between glasses until they all sit level — that level is the average.
explain: Average = total ÷ count. To find a missing value, work back from the total. When every number changes by the same amount, the average changes by that amount.
formulas: New value = (new avg × new n) − old sum

variant.q: Average of 5 numbers is 18. Adding a 6th number 30 makes the new average?

name: Time & Work
analogy: Filling a bucket together — each worker pours in their share of water per minute, so you add their rates. If A finishes in n days, A does 1/n of the job each day.
explain: Think in work-per-day. Add rates when people work together; men × days stays constant for the same job.

variant.q: A does a job in 15 days, B in 10 days. Together?

name: Pipes & Cisterns
analogy: A bathtub filling while the drain leaks — the net speed is the fill rate minus the leak rate. A draining pipe is just negative work.
explain: Identical to time & work, but an emptying pipe subtracts. Add all inflow rates and subtract outflow rates to get the net rate.

variant.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 h; pipe B empties it in 8 h. With both open?

name: Time, Speed & Distance / Trains
analogy: Passing a pole, a train travels exactly its own length; passing a platform, its length plus the platform's. Speed is just distance per unit time.
explain: Speed = distance ÷ time. Convert km/h to m/s with ×5/18. Opposite directions add speeds; same direction subtract.

variant.q: A train 200 m long at 36 km/h crosses a pole in?

name: Ages
analogy: A family photo timeline — everyone ages by the same number of years together. Set today's age as a letter, then shift by ±years.
explain: Let the present age be a variable; write past and future ages as ± years, then turn each ratio statement into an equation.
formulas: After t years: every age + t
Before t years: every age − t
Form equations from the ratios given

variant.q: A father is 3 times his son's age; in 12 years he will be twice. Son's present age?

name: Arithmetic Progression
analogy: Stairs of equal height — each step adds the same amount. The n-th term is the first plus (n−1) steps.
explain: An AP adds a constant step d. Count terms with (last−first)/d + 1; sum with n/2 × (first + last). Salary-increment problems are APs in disguise.

variant.q: Find the 10th term of 5, 8, 11, …

name: Algebra (identities, roots, indices)
analogy: A factor (x−k) is a key: x = k unlocks the expression to zero. Identities are shortcuts that skip the long multiplication.
explain: Use identities for cubes and squares; the remainder theorem says (x−k) is a factor when x=k gives 0. For a quadratic, product of roots = c/a and the discriminant is b²−4ac.

variant.q: If x + 1/x = 3, find x² + 1/x².

name: Probability
analogy: Drawing a coloured ball from a bag — count the balls you want over all the balls there are.
explain: Probability = favourable ÷ total outcomes. For 'at least one', it is easier to do 1 minus the probability of none.
formulas: Leap year: 2 extra days ⇒ 2/7 for any weekday

variant.q: A die is rolled. Probability of a number greater than 4?

name: Set Theory & Surveys
analogy: Two overlapping circles — add both groups but subtract the shared middle once, or you count it twice.
explain: Use n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B). 'Neither' equals the total minus those in at least one set.
formulas: At least one = A + B − both

variant.q: In a class of 50, 30 play cricket, 25 football, 10 both. How many play neither?

name: Mensuration — 2D
analogy: The same piece of string can be bent into a square or a circle; both keep the string's length as their perimeter. That is the link in most wire problems.
explain: Know area and perimeter of flat shapes. A wire bent into a shape keeps the same total length. A sector is a fraction of the full circle by its angle.

variant.q: A wire bent into a circle of radius 7 cm is reshaped into a square. Its side? (π=22/7)

name: Mensuration — 3D
analogy: The longest umbrella that fits in a room goes corner-to-corner — that is the space diagonal. Melting one solid into another keeps the volume the same.
explain: Volume and surface of solids. The longest rod in a box is the space diagonal √(l²+b²+h²). Melting conserves volume, so equate the volumes.
formulas: Cone V = ⅓ πr²h, Cylinder V = πr²h

variant.q: Longest rod that fits in a cubical room of edge 6 m?

name: Trigonometry & Heights
analogy: Your shadow equals your height exactly when the sun sits at 45°. Heights-and-distances problems are just tan = opposite / adjacent.
explain: Use tan = opposite/adjacent for towers, poles and ladders. If the two angles of elevation are complementary, the height is √(d₁·d₂).

variant.q: From 30 m away the top of a tower has elevation 30°. Height of tower?

name: Mixtures & Alligation
analogy: Adding water to squash dilutes it — the syrup stays the same, only the water grows. Track each ingredient's actual amount, then re-form the ratio.
explain: Convert the ratio to real quantities, adjust for what is added or removed, then write the new ratio.
formulas: Find actual quantities from the ratio
Re-form the ratio with new totals

variant.q: In 40 L of milk-water (3:1), how much water makes it 1:1?
variant.solution: Milk 30, water 10; need water 30 ⇒ add 20 L.

name: Partnership
analogy: A shared taxi — you pay for how much you ride AND how long you ride. Profit splits in the ratio of capital × time.
explain: Each partner's share is proportional to capital multiplied by the months invested.
formulas: Sum the ratio, find one part, scale

variant.q: A invests ₹5000 for 12 months, B ₹6000 for 10 months. Profit-share ratio?

name: Data Interpretation
analogy: A pie slice's angle is its share of the whole pie. If a 36° slice is ₹1600, the whole pie scales up from there.
explain: Read pie charts by angle (360° = whole), bars and lines by height. Percentage change compares to the earlier value.
formulas: Average bar = sum of bars ÷ count

variant.q: In a pie chart a 90° sector is 250 students. Total students?

name: Statistics (mean, median, mode)
analogy: The median is the person standing exactly in the middle of a queue sorted by height — sort first, then look at the centre.
explain: Mean is the average; median is the middle value after sorting; mode is the most frequent. They are linked by the empirical formula.
formulas: Median class: where cumulative freq passes N/2

variant.q: Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.

name: Coordinate Geometry
analogy: Walking across a grid: go along, then up — the straight-line distance is the hypotenuse of that right triangle.
explain: Distance between two points uses Pythagoras on the coordinate gaps.

variant.q: Distance between (0,0) and (3,4)?

name: Permutations & Combinations
analogy: A podium (1st / 2nd / 3rd) is a permutation because order matters; picking a team is a combination because it does not.
explain: Permutation counts arrangements (order matters); combination counts selections (order ignored). Arrangements of n distinct items = n!.

variant.q: In how many ways can 4 people sit in a row?
